topic: std::set::insert Return Value Semantics for Uniqueness
explanation:
For unique ordered associative containers (`std::set`, `std::map`), the standard library provides a specific return type for the single-argument `insert(const value_type&)` overload: `std::pair<iterator, bool>`.

Definition:
1. The `iterator` component (accessible via `.first`) always points to the element in the container, regardless of whether it was newly inserted or already existed.
2. The `bool` component (accessible via `.second`) indicates success: `true` if the insertion occurred (the element was new), and `false` if the insertion failed because an equivalent element already existed (due to the uniqueness constraint of the container).

Purpose: This structure allows the caller to atomically check for existence and obtain the iterator to the element (either the newly inserted one or the pre-existing one) in a single O(log N) operation, which is critical for efficient conditional logic.

Technical Details: The complexity of this operation is logarithmic, O(log N), corresponding to the tree traversal required to locate the insertion point or the existing element. This mechanism contrasts with `std::multiset::insert`, which returns only an iterator, as multisets do not enforce uniqueness and insertion always succeeds.

Pitfalls: Misinterpreting the iterator component when the boolean is false. The iterator still provides a valid reference to the pre-existing element, not an end iterator or an invalidated position.
practical_example: Managing a cache of configuration objects identified by a unique key. Using the `pair` return value allows the system to check if a configuration already exists in the cache; if not, it inserts the new object, and in either case, it immediately obtains the iterator to the active object for subsequent use, avoiding a secondary lookup operation.
book: The C++ Standard Library: A Tutorial and Reference by Nicolai M. Josuttis
